tip: Nouns ending in '-ing' normally drop the 'g' and take '-kje' in the diminutive: 'ketting' becomes 'kettinkje'.
After a short vowel plus 'r', the diminutive doubles the 'r' and adds '-etje': 'ster' becomes 'sterretje'.
'Meenemen' is separable: the prefix 'mee' moves to the end, leaving 'nemen ... mee' around the object.
After a long vowel plus 'l', 'n' or 'r', the diminutive just adds '-tje': 'verhaal' becomes 'verhaaltje'.
For listen to, 'luisteren' takes the preposition 'naar': 'luisteren naar een liedje'.
For that or who, a 'het' word takes 'dat' and a 'de' word takes 'die': 'het kind dat zijn huiswerk vergat'.
'Les geven', literally give lessons, is the everyday way to say to teach: 'de leraar die mij les gaf'.
'Zou' plus a past participle plus 'hebben' means would have done: 'zou het niet gedaan hebben'.
When something else comes first, the main verb stays in the second slot, before the subject: 'vergeet ik nooit'.
'Er wordt' plus a past participle describes an action with no named doer: 'er wordt gezegd' = it is said.
'Ik wil' can sound blunt, so soften a request with 'ik zou graag ... willen': 'Ik zou graag meer willen weten' (I would like to know more).
For a machine that refuses to work, Dutch uses 'willen': 'zijn auto niet wilde starten' = his car would not start.
After a comparative, than is 'dan': 'Amsterdam is groter dan Utrecht'.
'Wegens' is a formal because of and is followed by a noun: 'gesloten wegens verbouwing'.
'Een praatje maken', literally make a chat, means to have a quick chat: 'hij maakt een praatje'.
'Per' names a means of transport with no article after it: 'per boot' = by boat.
'Zetten' places something upright, where 'leggen' would lay it flat: 'zij zet een plantje op de vensterbank'.
For a thing, join 'waar' to the preposition: 'waarvoor' means for which, as in 'het bedrijf waarvoor ik werk'.
'Zich opmaken' keeps its 'zich' and is separable: the 'op' splits off to the end, giving 'maakt zich op'.
The superlative normally adds '-ste' and takes 'de' or 'het': 'slim' becomes 'de slimste leerling'.
'Waarvoor' (for which) can split in two: 'het probleem waar niemand een oplossing voor had'. The split version is the informal, spoken style.
'Valt' plus 'te' and an infinitive expresses what can be done: 'er valt niets meer aan te doen' = nothing more can be done about it.
'Behalve' at the start means except or apart from: 'behalve maandag' = except Monday.
Use 'die' for who or that after a 'de' word: 'de man die daar staat'.
For a thing, Dutch joins 'waar' to the preposition: 'waarnaast' means next to which, as in 'het huis waarnaast wij wonen'.
In the clause after 'die', the verbs move to the end: 'de film die wij hebben gezien'.
'Er' lets an indefinite subject follow the verb: 'er spelen kinderen' = there are children playing.
In a passive, 'door' marks who or what does the action: 'wordt gesproken door meer dan twintig miljoen mensen'.
'Want' means because but keeps normal word order, verb second: 'want ik heb het meegemaakt'.
In a music context 'nummer' means a track or song, not just number: 'het nummer dat op de radio speelt'.
